On Arithmetical Structures on Complete Graphs

Zachary Harris Z. HarrisDepartment of Mathematics, Niagara University, Niagara University, NY 14109, USA Email address: zharris.edu@gmail.com and Joel Louwsma J. LouwsmaDepartment of Mathematics, Niagara University, Niagara University, NY 14109, USA Email address: jlouwsma@niagara.edu
Abstract.

An arithmetical structure on the complete graph KnK_{n} with nn vertices is given by a collection of nn positive integers with no common factor each of which divides their sum. We show that, for all positive integers cc less than a certain bound depending on nn, there is an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n} with largest value cc. We also show that, if each prime factor of cc is greater than (n+1)2/4(n+1)^{2}/4, there is no arithmetical structure on KnK_{n} with largest value cc. We apply these results to study which prime numbers can occur as the largest value of an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n}.

1. Introduction

How can one have a collection of positive integers, with no common factor, each of which divides their sum? For example, 105105, 7070, 1515, 1414, and 66 sum to 210210, which is divisible by each of these numbers. Introducing notation, we seek positive integers r1,r2,…,rnr_{1},r_{2},\dotsc,r_{n} with no common factor such that

(1) rj|∑i=1nrifor all j.r_{j}\,\,\Big|\,\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}\quad\text{for all~$j$.}

It is well known that finding such rir_{i} is equivalent to finding positive integer solutions of the Diophantine equation

(2) 1x1+1x2+⋯+1xn=1.\frac{1}{x_{1}}+\frac{1}{x_{2}}+\dotsb+\frac{1}{x_{n}}=1.

Indeed, given r1,r2,…,rnr_{1},r_{2},\dotsc,r_{n} satisfying (1), dividing both sides of the equation r1+r2+⋯+rn=∑i=1nrir_{1}+r_{2}+\dotsb+r_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i} by ∑i=1nri\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i} gives a solution to (2), and, given a solution of (2), the numbers lcm⁡(x1,x2,…,xn)/xi\lcm(x_{1},x_{2},\dotsc,x_{n})/x_{i} satisfy (1) and have no common factor.

Our interest in this question stems from an interest in arithmetical structures. An arithmetical structure on a finite, connected graph is an assignment of positive integers to the vertices such that:

  1. (a)

    At each vertex, the integer there is a divisor of the sum of the integers at adjacent vertices (counted with multiplicity if the graph is not simple).

  2. (b)

    The integers used have no nontrivial common factor.

Arithmetical structures were introduced by Lorenzini [14] to study intersections of degenerating curves in algebraic geometry. The usual definition, easily seen to be equivalent to the one given here, is formulated in terms of matrices. From that perspective, an arithmetical structure may be regarded as a generalization of the Laplacian matrix, which encodes many important properties of a graph. Notions in this direction that have received a significant amount of attention include the sandpile group and the chip-firing game; for details, see [8, 12, 10].

On the complete graph KnK_{n} with nn vertices, positive integers r1,r2,…,rnr_{1},r_{2},\dotsc,r_{n} with no common factor give an arithmetical structure if and only if

rj|∑i=1i≠jnrifor all j;r_{j}\,\,\Big|\,\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i=1\\ i\neq j\end{subarray}}^{n}r_{i}\quad\text{for all~$j$};

it is immediate that this condition is equivalent to (1). Therefore, in this language, the opening question of this paper seeks arithmetical structures on complete graphs.

Lorenzini [14, Lemma 1.6] shows that there are finitely many arithmetical structures on any finite, connected graph, but his result does not give a bound on the number of structures. Several recent papers [3, 2, 11] count arithmetical structures on various families of graphs, including path graphs, cycle graphs, bidents, and certain path graphs with doubled edges. However, counting arithmetical structures on complete graphs is a difficult problem. The number of arithmetical structures on KnK_{n} for n≤8n\leq 8 is given in [15]. For general nn, bounds have been obtained by several authors [9, 16, 4, 13] working from the perspective of the Diophantine equation (2). Other papers such as [5, 6, 1] determine, for specific nn, the number of solutions of (2) satisfying certain additional conditions on the xix_{i}.

It is conjectured in [7, Conjecture 6.10] that, for any connected, simple graph GG with nn vertices, the number of arithmetical structures on GG is at most the number of arithmetical structures on KnK_{n}. To approach this conjecture, one would like a better understanding of the types of arithmetical structures that occur on complete graphs. In this direction, this paper studies which positive integers can occur as the largest value of an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n}. Clearly the rir_{i} of an arithmetical structure can be permuted; in the following we make the assumption r1≥r2≥⋯≥rnr_{1}\geq r_{2}\geq\dotsb\geq r_{n}. We construct arithmetical structures to show that r1r_{1} can take certain values and give obstructions to show that it cannot take other values.

Our primary construction theorem (Theorem 1) shows that r1r_{1} can take any value up to a certain bound depending on nn. More specifically, r1r_{1} can be any positive integer less than or equal to maxk∈ℤ>0⁡(2k​n−(k+2k−2)​2k−1)\max_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}}(2^{k}n-(k+2^{k}-2)2^{k}-1). This bound improves somewhat if we restrict attention to prime numbers; r1r_{1} can be any prime number less than or equal to maxk∈ℤ>0⁡(2k​n−(k+2k−3)​2k−3)\max_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}}(2^{k}n-(k+2^{k}-3)2^{k}-3).

We also prove an obstruction theorem (Theorem 7) that shows r1r_{1} cannot take any value all of whose prime factors are greater than (n+1)2/4(n+1)^{2}/4. Restricting attention to prime numbers, this bound improves to show that r1r_{1} cannot be any prime number greater than n2/4+1n^{2}/4+1 (Theorem 8).

The final section focuses on the possible prime values r1r_{1} can take. We explicitly check prime numbers in the gap between the bound of Theorem 1 and the bound of Theorem 8, showing that r1r_{1} can take some of these values but not others. In particular, we observe that there can be prime numbers p1p_{1} and p2p_{2} with p1<p2p_{1}<p_{2} such that there is an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n} with r1=p2r_{1}=p_{2} but no arithmetical structure on KnK_{n} with r1=p1r_{1}=p_{1}.

2. Construction

In this section, we show how to construct arithmetical structures on complete graphs with certain values of r1r_{1}. Our main construction theorem is the following.

Theorem 1.
  1. (a)

    For any positive integer c≤maxk∈ℤ>0⁡(2k​n−(k+2k−2)​2k−1)c\leq\max_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}}(2^{k}n-(k+2^{k}-2)2^{k}-1), there is an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n} with r1=cr_{1}=c.

  2. (b)

    For any prime number p≤maxk∈ℤ>0⁡(2k​n−(k+2k−3)​2k−3)p\leq\max_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}}(2^{k}n-(k+2^{k}-3)2^{k}-3), there is an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n} with r1=pr_{1}=p.

We establish Propositions 2, 4, and 5 on the way to proving Theorem 1.

Proposition 2.

For any positive integer c≤n−1c\leq n-1, there is an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n} with r1=cr_{1}=c.

Proof.

Let

ri={cfor ​i∈{1,2,…,n−c},1for ​i∈{n−c+1,n−c+2,…,n}.r_{i}=\begin{cases}c&\text{for }i\in\{1,2,\dotsc,n-c\},\\ 1&\text{for }i\in\{n-c+1,n-c+2,\dotsc,n\}.\end{cases}

Then

∑i=1nri=c⁡(n−c)+c=c⁡(n−c+1).\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}=c(n-c)+c=c(n-c+1).

Since this is divisible by both cc and 11, we have thus produced an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n}. ∎

Before turning to Propositions 4 and 5, we establish the following lemma.

Lemma 3.
  1. (a)

    Let k∈ℤ≥0k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} and ℓ∈ℤ>0\ell\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0} with k≤ℓk\leq\ell. Every integer cc satisfying ℓ≤c≤(ℓ−k+1)​2k−1\ell\leq c\leq(\ell-k+1)2^{k}-1 can be expressed as ∑j=1ℓ2kj\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}2^{k_{j}} for some kj∈{0,1,…,k}k_{j}\in\{0,1,\dotsc,k\}, where kj=0k_{j}=0 for some j∈{1,2,…,ℓ}j\in\{1,2,\dotsc,\ell\}.

  2. (b)

    Let k∈ℤ≥0k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} and ℓ∈ℤ>0\ell\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0} with k≤ℓk\leq\ell. Every odd integer cc satisfying ℓ≤c≤(ℓ−k+2)​2k−3\ell\leq c\leq(\ell-k+2)2^{k}-3 can be expressed as ∑j=1ℓ2kj\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}2^{k_{j}} for some kj∈{0,1,…,k}k_{j}\in\{0,1,\dotsc,k\}, where kj=0k_{j}=0 for some j∈{1,2,…,ℓ}j\in\{1,2,\dotsc,\ell\}.

Proof.

To show (a), we proceed by induction on cc. In the base case, c=ℓc=\ell, we can let kj=0k_{j}=0 for all jj and have c=∑j=1ℓ2kjc=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}2^{k_{j}}. Now suppose c=∑j=1ℓ2kjc=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}2^{k_{j}} for c≤(ℓ−k+1)​2k−2c\leq(\ell-k+1)2^{k}-2. Then kj=kk_{j}=k for at most ℓ−k\ell-k values of jj, meaning kj<kk_{j}<k for at least kk values of jj. If among these values we had each of 0,1,…,k−10,1,\dotsc,k-1 only once, we would then have ∑j=1ℓ2kj=(ℓ−k+1)​2k−1>(ℓ−k+1)​2k−2\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}2^{k_{j}}=(\ell-k+1)2^{k}-1>(\ell-k+1)2^{k}-2. Therefore there is some b<kb<k for which kj1=b=kj2k_{j_{1}}=b=k_{j_{2}} for some j1≠j2j_{1}\neq j_{2}. Define

kj′={kj+1for ​j=j1,0for ​j=j2,kjotherwise.k_{j}^{\prime}=\begin{cases}k_{j}+1&\text{for }j=j_{1},\\ 0&\text{for }j=j_{2},\\ k_{j}&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

Then ∑j=1ℓ2kj′=∑j=1ℓ2kj+1=c+1\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}2^{k_{j}^{\prime}}=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}2^{k_{j}}+1=c+1. The result follows.

For (b), first note that if c≤(ℓ−k+1)​2k−1c\leq(\ell-k+1)2^{k}-1 then the result follows from (a). Therefore, assume c>(ℓ−k+1)​2k−1c>(\ell-k+1)2^{k}-1 and let c′=c−((ℓ−k+1)​2k−1)c^{\prime}=c-((\ell-k+1)2^{k}-1), noting that c′≤2k−2c^{\prime}\leq 2^{k}-2. Since cc is odd, c′c^{\prime} must be even. Therefore c′c^{\prime} can be written in the form ∑j=1k−1sj​2j\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}s_{j}2^{j}, where each sjs_{j} is either 00 or 11; the sjs_{j} are iteratively determined in reverse by letting sj=1s_{j}=1 if c′−∑i=j+1k−1si​2i≥2jc^{\prime}-\sum_{i=j+1}^{k-1}s_{i}2^{i}\geq 2^{j} and letting sj=0s_{j}=0 otherwise. Define

kj={0for ​j=1,j−1+sj−1for ​j∈{2,3,…,k},kfor ​j∈{k+1,k+2,…,ℓ}.k_{j}=\begin{cases}0&\text{for }j=1,\\ j-1+s_{j-1}&\text{for }j\in\{2,3,\dotsc,k\},\\ k&\text{for }j\in\{k+1,k+2,\dotsc,\ell\}.\end{cases}

Then

∑j=1ℓ2kj=∑j=1k2j−1+∑j=2ksj−1​2j−1+∑j=k+1ℓ2k=2k−1+c′+(ℓ−k)​2k=c.∎\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}2^{k_{j}}=\sum_{j=1}^{k}2^{j-1}+\sum_{j=2}^{k}s_{j-1}2^{j-1}+\sum_{j=k+1}^{\ell}2^{k}=2^{k}-1+c^{\prime}+(\ell-k)2^{k}=c.\qed

We use Lemma 3 to prove Propositions 4 and 5.

Proposition 4.

Fix n≥2n\geq 2. For any positive integer kk satisfying k+2k−1≤nk+2^{k}-1\leq n and any positive integer cc satisfying n−2k+1≤c≤(n−k−2k+2)​2k−1n-2^{k}+1\leq c\leq(n-k-2^{k}+2)2^{k}-1, there is an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n} with r1=cr_{1}=c.

Proof.

Let ri=cr_{i}=c for all i∈{1,2,…,2k−1}i\in\{1,2,\dotsc,2^{k}-1\}. Let ℓ=n−2k+1\ell=n-2^{k}+1, noting that our assumptions guarantee that k≤ℓk\leq\ell and ℓ≤c≤(ℓ−k+1)​2k−1\ell\leq c\leq(\ell-k+1)2^{k}-1. Lemma 3(a) then shows how to write c=∑j=1ℓ2kjc=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}2^{k_{j}}. We use the values 2kj2^{k_{j}}, in decreasing order, to define rir_{i} for i∈{2k,2k+1,…,n}i\in\{2^{k},2^{k}+1,\dotsc,n\}, noting that rn=1r_{n}=1. Then

∑i=1nri=(2k−1)​c+c=2k​c.\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}=(2^{k}-1)c+c=2^{k}c.

Since 2k​c2^{k}c is divisible by cc and by 2k′2^{k^{\prime}} for all k′∈{0,1,…,k}k^{\prime}\in\{0,1,\dotsc,k\}, we have thus produced an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n}. ∎

Although we imposed the condition k+2k−1≤nk+2^{k}-1\leq n here to ensure that k≤ℓk\leq\ell in the proof, this does not restrict possible values of r1r_{1}, as we show in the proof of Theorem 1. Together with Proposition 2, Proposition 4 with k=1k=1 allows us to construct arithmetical structures on KnK_{n} with r1r_{1} taking any value up to 2​n−32n-3. When k=2k=2, the bound is 4​n−174n-17; when k=3k=3, the bound is 8​n−738n-73; and when k=4k=4, the bound is 16​n−28916n-289. If we restrict attention to prime r1r_{1}, these bounds can be improved slightly, as the following proposition shows.

Proposition 5.

Fix n≥2n\geq 2. For any positive integer kk satisfying k+2k−1≤nk+2^{k}-1\leq n and any prime number pp satisfying n−2k+1≤p≤(n−k−2k+3)​2k−3n-2^{k}+1\leq p\leq(n-k-2^{k}+3)2^{k}-3, there is an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n} with r1=pr_{1}=p.

Proof.

If p=2p=2 (and n≥3n\geq 3), Proposition 2 gives an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n} with r1=pr_{1}=p. Therefore suppose pp is odd. Let ri=pr_{i}=p for all i∈{1,2,…,2k−1}i\in\{1,2,\dotsc,2^{k}-1\}. Let ℓ=n−2k+1\ell=n-2^{k}+1, noting that our assumptions guarantee k≤ℓk\leq\ell and ℓ≤p≤(ℓ−k+2)​2k−3\ell\leq p\leq(\ell-k+2)2^{k}-3. Lemma 3(b) then shows how to write p=∑j=1ℓ2kjp=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}2^{k_{j}}. As in the proof of Proposition 4, we use the values 2kj2^{k_{j}}, in decreasing order, to define rir_{i} for i∈{2k,2k+1,…,n}i\in\{2^{k},2^{k}+1,\dotsc,n\}, noting that rn=1r_{n}=1. Then

∑i=1nri=(2k−1)​p+p=2k​p,\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}=(2^{k}-1)p+p=2^{k}p,

which is divisible by pp and by 2k′2^{k^{\prime}} for all k′∈{0,1,…,k}k^{\prime}\in\{0,1,\dotsc,k\}, so therefore we have produced an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n}. ∎

For example, when k=1k=1, Proposition 5 allows us to construct arithmetical structures on KnK_{n} with r1r_{1} taking prime values as large as 2​n−32n-3. When k=2k=2, the bound is 4​n−154n-15; when k=3k=3, the bound is 8​n−678n-67; and when k=4k=4, the bound is 16​n−27516n-275.

We are now prepared to complete the proof of Theorem 1.

Proof of Theorem 1.

The necessary constructions are given in Propositions 2, 4, and 5. It remains only to show that, for each nn, values of kk that maximize the upper bounds in Propositions 4 and 5 satisfy k+2k−1≤nk+2^{k}-1\leq n.

The upper bound (n−k−2k+2)​2k−1(n-k-2^{k}+2)2^{k}-1 in Proposition 4 is linear in nn with slope 2k2^{k}. A straightforward calculation shows that the bound with slope 2k−12^{k-1} coincides with the bound with slope 2k2^{k} when n=k+3⋅2k−1−1n=k+3\cdot 2^{k-1}-1 and that the bound with slope 2k2^{k} coincides with the bound with slope 2k+12^{k+1} when n=k+3⋅2kn=k+3\cdot 2^{k}. Therefore the bound with slope 2k2^{k} is maximal exactly when nn is between k+3⋅2k−1−1k+3\cdot 2^{k-1}-1 and k+3⋅2kk+3\cdot 2^{k}. When the bound is maximized, we therefore have that n≥k+3⋅2k−1−1≥k+2k−1n\geq k+3\cdot 2^{k-1}-1\geq k+2^{k}-1, meaning the condition of Proposition 4 is satisfied. This proves (a).

The argument for (b) is very similar. The upper bound (n−k−2k+3)​2k−3(n-k-2^{k}+3)2^{k}-3 in Proposition 5 is maximal for nn between k+3⋅2k−1−2k+3\cdot 2^{k-1}-2 and k+3⋅2k−1k+3\cdot 2^{k}-1. When the bound is maximized, we then have that n≥k+3⋅2k−1−2≥k+2k−1n\geq k+3\cdot 2^{k-1}-2\geq k+2^{k}-1, meaning the condition of Proposition 5 is satisfied. ∎

We conclude this section by giving another construction that allows us to produce some arithmetical structures with values of r1r_{1} other than those guaranteed by Theorem 1.

Proposition 6.

For any positive integer k≤n−1k\leq n-1, there is an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n} with r1=k⁡(n−k)+1r_{1}=k(n-k)+1.

Proof.

Let

ri={k⁡(n−k)+1for ​i∈{1,2,…,k−1},kfor ​i∈{k,k+1,…,n−1},1for ​i=n.r_{i}=\begin{cases}k(n-k)+1&\text{for }i\in\{1,2,\dotsc,k-1\},\\ k&\text{for }i\in\{k,k+1,\dotsc,n-1\},\\ 1&\text{for }i=n.\end{cases}

Then

∑i=1nri=(k−1)​(k⁡(n−k)+1)+k⁡(n−k)+1=k⁡(k⁡(n−k)+1).\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}=(k-1)(k(n-k)+1)+k(n-k)+1=k(k(n-k)+1).

Since this is divisible by k⁡(n−k)+1k(n-k)+1, kk, and 11, we have thus produced an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n}. ∎

For example, when n=13n=13, Theorem 1 guarantees that we can find an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n} with r1=pr_{1}=p for all prime p≤37p\leq 37. By taking k=5k=5 in Proposition 6, we can also produce an arithmetical structure with r1=41r_{1}=41. By taking k=6k=6, we can produce an arithmetical structure with r1=43r_{1}=43. The results of this section cannot be extended too much further, as we show in the following section.

3. Obstruction

We next prove obstruction results that complement our constructions in the previous section. Our first result shows that r1r_{1} cannot be a product of primes all of which are too large.

Theorem 7.

Suppose c≥2c\geq 2 is an integer with prime factorization p1a1​p2a2​⋯​pkakp_{1}^{a_{1}}p_{2}^{a_{2}}\dotsm p_{k}^{a_{k}}, where p1<p2<⋯<pkp_{1}<p_{2}<\dotsb<p_{k} and ai≥1a_{i}\geq 1 for all ii. If p1>(n+1)2/4p_{1}>(n+1)^{2}/4, then there is no arithmetical structure on KnK_{n} with r1=cr_{1}=c.

Proof.

Suppose we have an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n} with r1=cr_{1}=c. Knowing that r1|∑i=1nrir_{1}\mid\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}, we define b=∑i=1nri/r1b=\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}/r_{1}. Then ∑i=1nri=b​c\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}=bc, meaning that ri|b​p1a1​p2a2​⋯​pkakr_{i}\mid bp_{1}^{a_{1}}p_{2}^{a_{2}}\dotsm p_{k}^{a_{k}} for all ii. Let mm be the largest value of ii for which ri=cr_{i}=c. For all i∈{m+1,m+2​…,n}i\in\{m+1,m+2\dotsc,n\}, we have ri<cr_{i}<c, which implies that ri≤b​p1a1−1​p2a2​⋯​pkakr_{i}\leq bp_{1}^{a_{1}-1}p_{2}^{a_{2}}\dotsm p_{k}^{a_{k}}. This means ∑i=m+1nri≤(n−m)​b​p1a1−1​p2a2​⋯​pkak\sum_{i=m+1}^{n}r_{i}\leq(n-m)bp_{1}^{a_{1}-1}p_{2}^{a_{2}}\dotsm p_{k}^{a_{k}}. We also have that ∑i=m+1nri=(b−m)​p1a1​p2a2​⋯​pkak\sum_{i=m+1}^{n}r_{i}=(b-m)p_{1}^{a_{1}}p_{2}^{a_{2}}\dotsm p_{k}^{a_{k}}. Therefore

(b−m)​p1a1​p2a2​⋯​pkak≤(n−m)​b​p1a1−1​p2a2​⋯​pkak,(b-m)p_{1}^{a_{1}}p_{2}^{a_{2}}\dotsm p_{k}^{a_{k}}\leq(n-m)bp_{1}^{a_{1}-1}p_{2}^{a_{2}}\dotsm p_{k}^{a_{k}},

and hence (b−m)​p1≤(n−m)​b(b-m)p_{1}\leq(n-m)b. When b=mb=m, there is only one arithmetical structure on KnK_{n}, namely that with ri=1r_{i}=1 for all ii, so the desired structure cannot arise in this case. Therefore we assume b>mb>m, in which case we have

p1≤(n−m)​bb−m.p_{1}\leq\frac{(n-m)b}{b-m}.

When b=m+1b=m+1, this gives p1≤(n−b+1)​bp_{1}\leq(n-b+1)b. It is a simple calculus exercise to show this bound is maximized when b=(n+1)/2b=(n+1)/2. It follows that p1≤(n+1)2/4p_{1}\leq(n+1)^{2}/4.

When b≥m+2b\geq m+2, we have that

p1≤(n−m)​bb−m=n​b−m​b+n​m−n​mb−m=n+m⁡(n−b)b−m≤n+m⁡(n−m−2)2.p_{1}\leq\frac{(n-m)b}{b-m}=\frac{nb-mb+nm-nm}{b-m}=n+\frac{m(n-b)}{b-m}\leq n+\frac{m(n-m-2)}{2}.

It is a simple calculus exercise to show this bound is maximized when m=n/2−1m=n/2-1, so therefore

p1≤n+(n/2−1)​(n/2−1)2=n28+n2+12=(n+1)24−n2−14≤(n+1)24.p_{1}\leq n+\frac{(n/2-1)(n/2-1)}{2}=\frac{n^{2}}{8}+\frac{n}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{(n+1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{n^{2}-1}{4}\leq\frac{(n+1)^{2}}{4}.

The result follows. ∎

If we restrict attention to arithmetical structures where r1r_{1} is a prime number, then Theorem 7 can be improved to Theorem 8. The general outline of the proof is similar, with some of the bounds improved.

Theorem 8.

If pp is a prime number with p>n2/4+1p>n^{2}/4+1, then there is no arithmetical structure on KnK_{n} with r1=pr_{1}=p.

Proof.

If p=2p=2, the hypothesis of the theorem is only satisfied for n=1n=1, and there is no arithmetical structure on K1K_{1} with r1=2r_{1}=2. Suppose we have an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n} with r1=pr_{1}=p, where p≥3p\geq 3. Knowing that r1|∑i=1nrir_{1}\mid\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}, we define b=∑i=1nri/r1b=\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}/r_{1}. Then ∑i=1nri=b​p\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}=bp, meaning that ri|b​pr_{i}\mid bp for all ii. Let mm be the largest value of ii for which ri=pr_{i}=p. We can only have b=mb=m if ri=1r_{i}=1 for all ii, but then r1r_{1} is not prime. We consider two cases: when b=m+1b=m+1 and when b≥m+2b\geq m+2.

Case I: b=m+1b=m+1. For all i∈{m+1,m+2,…,n}i\in\{m+1,m+2,\dotsc,n\}, we have that ri|b​pr_{i}\mid bp and ri<pr_{i}<p, so therefore ri|br_{i}\mid b. Whenever ri<br_{i}<b, this means ri≤b/2r_{i}\leq b/2. If rn−1,rn<br_{n-1},r_{n}<b, we would then have that ∑i=m+1nri≤(n−m−1)​b\sum_{i=m+1}^{n}r_{i}\leq(n-m-1)b. If instead ri=br_{i}=b for all i∈{m+1,m+2,…,n−1}i\in\{m+1,m+2,\dotsc,n-1\}, we would have that rn|rir_{n}\mid r_{i} for all i∈{m+1,m+2,…,n}i\in\{m+1,m+2,\dotsc,n\}. Since ∑i=m+1nri=(b−m)​p=p\sum_{i=m+1}^{n}r_{i}=(b-m)p=p, this would also mean rn|pr_{n}\mid p, and hence that rn|rir_{n}\mid r_{i} for all ii. Therefore we would need to have rn=1r_{n}=1, meaning that ∑i=m+1nri≤(n−m−1)​b+1\sum_{i=m+1}^{n}r_{i}\leq(n-m-1)b+1. Regardless of the value of rn−1r_{n-1}, we thus have that

p=∑i=m+1nri≤(n−m−1)​b+1=(n−b)​b+1=n​b−b2+1.p=\sum_{i=m+1}^{n}r_{i}\leq(n-m-1)b+1=(n-b)b+1=nb-b^{2}+1.

It is a simple calculus exercise to show that this bound is maximized when b=n/2b=n/2. Hence we have that p≤n2/4+1p\leq n^{2}/4+1.

Case II: b≥m+2b\geq m+2. We have that ri≤br_{i}\leq b for all i∈{m+1,m+2,…,n}i\in\{m+1,m+2,\dotsc,n\} and ∑i=m+1nri=(b−m)​p\sum_{i=m+1}^{n}r_{i}=(b-m)p, so therefore (b−m)​p≤(n−m)​b(b-m)p\leq(n-m)b. As in the proof of Theorem 7, this yields that

p≤(n−m)​bb−m≤n+m⁡(n−m−2)2,p\leq\frac{(n-m)b}{b-m}\leq n+\frac{m(n-m-2)}{2},

and this bound is maximized when m=n/2−1m=n/2-1. Therefore

p≤n+(n/2−1)​(n/2−1)2=n28+n2+12=n24+1−(n−2)28<n24+1.p\leq n+\frac{(n/2-1)(n/2-1)}{2}=\frac{n^{2}}{8}+\frac{n}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{n^{2}}{4}+1-\frac{(n-2)^{2}}{8}<\frac{n^{2}}{4}+1.

We have thus shown that in all cases we must have p≤n2/4+1p\leq n^{2}/4+1. ∎

For even nn, we can choose k=n/2k=n/2 in Proposition 6 and get an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n} with r1=n2/4+1r_{1}=n^{2}/4+1. For odd nn, we can choose k=(n−1)/2k=(n-1)/2 and get an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n} with r1=(n2−1)/4+1r_{1}=(n^{2}-1)/4+1. As some of these values of r1r_{1} are prime, the bound in Theorem 8 therefore cannot be improved.

There are arithmetical structures for which r1r_{1} takes composite values larger than the bound given in Theorem 8. For instance, the example in the opening paragraph of this paper gives an arithmetical structure on K5K_{5} with r1=105r_{1}=105.

4. Prime r1r_{1}

This section considers the possible prime values r1r_{1} can take in an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n}. Theorem 1(b) guarantees that r1r_{1} can take any prime value up to 2k​n−(k+2k−3)​2k−32^{k}n-(k+2^{k}-3)2^{k}-3 for any kk. Theorem 8 says that r1r_{1} cannot take any prime value larger than n2/4+1n^{2}/4+1. These bounds are not too far from each other. The function n2/4+1n^{2}/4+1 has linear approximations of the form 2k​n−22​k+12^{k}n-2^{2k}+1. When kk is 11 or 22, this linear approximation coincides with the bound from Theorem 1(b). In general, it differs from this bound by (k−3)​2k+4(k-3)2^{k}+4.

Proposition 6 shows that r1r_{1} can take some of the prime values in the gap between the bound of Theorem 1(b) and the bound of Theorem 8. We can check by hand whether it can take other prime values; to illustrate how to do this, we explain why there is no arithmetical structure on K18K_{18} with r1=79r_{1}=79. Suppose there were such a structure, and let b=∑i=118ri/r1b=\sum_{i=1}^{18}r_{i}/r_{1}, so that ∑i=118ri=79​b\sum_{i=1}^{18}r_{i}=79b. Let mm be the largest value of ii for which ri=79r_{i}=79. Then ∑i=m+118ri=79​(b−m)\sum_{i=m+1}^{18}r_{i}=79(b-m). For all i∈{m+1,m+2,…,18}i\in\{m+1,m+2,\dotsc,18\}, we have that ri|79​br_{i}\mid 79b and ri<79r_{i}<79. Therefore ri|br_{i}\mid b, and hence ri≤br_{i}\leq b. This means that ∑i=m+118ri≤(18−m)​b\sum_{i=m+1}^{18}r_{i}\leq(18-m)b, so we must have 79​(b−m)≤(18−m)​b79(b-m)\leq(18-m)b. If b≥m+2b\geq m+2, we would have that

61​b−79​m+m​b≥61​(m+2)−79​m+m⁡(m+2)=(m−8)2+58>0,61b-79m+mb\geq 61(m+2)-79m+m(m+2)=(m-8)^{2}+58>0,

which would imply that 79​(b−m)>(18−m)​b79(b-m)>(18-m)b. Therefore we cannot have b≥m+2b\geq m+2. Since b=mb=m is only possible if r1=1r_{1}=1, it therefore remains to consider whether we can have b=m+1b=m+1. In this case, we would have ∑i=m+118ri≤(18−m)​(m+1)\sum_{i=m+1}^{18}r_{i}\leq(18-m)(m+1). This bound is less than 7979 except when mm satisfies 6≤m≤116\leq m\leq 11. If m=6m=6, we would need to have 1212 divisors of 77 that sum to 7979, but this is not possible. If m=7m=7, we would need to have 1111 divisors of 88 that sum to 7979, but this is not possible. If m=8m=8, we would need to have 1010 divisors of 99 that sum to 7979, but this is not possible. If m=9m=9, we would need to have 99 divisors of 1010 that sum to 7979, but this is not possible. If m=10m=10, we would need to have 88 divisors of 1111 that sum to 7979, but this is not possible. If m=11m=11, we would need to have 77 divisors of 1212 that sum to 7979, but this is not possible. Therefore there is no arithmetical structure on K18K_{18} with r1=79r_{1}=79. A similar approach can be used to either find arithmetical structures with other prime values of r1r_{1} or to show that they do not exist. We have done this for all n≤27n\leq 27; the results are shown in Table 1.

We conclude by noting that, on K27K_{27}, there is no arithmetical structure with r1=179r_{1}=179 whereas there is an arithmetical structure with r1=181r_{1}=181. This shows that there is not a cutoff function f⁡(n)f(n) such that, for each nn, there is an arithmetical structure on KnK_{n} with r1=pr_{1}=p for all primes p≤f⁡(n)p\leq f(n) and no such structure for any p>f⁡(n)p>f(n). Therefore, while one could attempt to improve the bound of Theorem 1(b), the possible prime values of r1r_{1} cannot be fully explained by a result of this form.
